articles.title_orig: Iran, China and Russia face new pressure from Trump
articles.title_zh: Iran, China and Russia face new pressure from Trump
articles.content_orig:
United States President Donald Trump is meeting with his Chinese and Russian counterparts for highly anticipated trilateral talks at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation ( APEC ) summit.
Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin began talks on the sidelines of the summit in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday in an unprecedented gathering of the world’s three superpowers.
The talks between the leaders of the world’s largest nuclear powers are unlikely to produce major agreements, analysts say, given deep differences over Ukraine, Iran, nuclear weapons and trade. But the meeting has unnerved smaller countries that fear their interests might be disregarded.
Ahead of the trilateral gathering, Trump held separate bilateral meetings with both Xi and Putin on Thursday.
The US president described Xi as a “friend” and said Washington and Beijing enjoyed a “special relationship”.
“As long as the two of us are in charge, I don’t think we’ll have a problem,” Trump said in opening remarks at his meeting with the Chinese leader. He also boasted that “no other countries can do what we can”.
Trump said the US has done “amazing” things in the past two years, since he returned to power, while praising China for many of its gains over several years.
Xi, meanwhile, said that he remained committed to working with Trump to steer ties between their countries on the “correct course”.
Relations between Beijing and Washington have been stable and improving, Xi said to Trump at the start of their third meeting this year, which lasted for about an hour.
“We have established a new definition of a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability, giving it new substance based on respect, fairness and reciprocity,” Xi said.
Ahead of the bilateral meeting, Trump said the Board of Trade that he and the Chinese president agreed to form at their Beijing summit in May has brought balance to the two countries’ relationship. He said the US and China had split their tariffs in a “fair way”.
Earlier in the day, during talks with Putin, Trump also called the Russian leader a “friend”.
“We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We know each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start. But I think they’ll come out of this,” Trump told Putin.
A video published by the White House showed the two leaders shaking hands and Trump briefly whispering to Putin at the start of their meeting.
In another video posted by the White House Rapid Response X account, Trump was shown pointing at Putin and saying, “He’s my friend.”
Kremlin foreign policy aide Yury Ushakov said the two leaders “discussed the conflict in Ukraine and bilateral relations issues”.
“The meeting between the Russian and US leaders went well,” Ushakov said, according to Russia’s state news agency TASS, adding that Putin left the talks “in an excellent” mood.
“There were no particularly significant statements made at the Putin-Trump talks; everyone is preparing for the trilateral meeting,” he added.
Thursday also features the main event of the APEC summit, as representatives of the 21 Pacific Rim economies gather for discussions that will include high-stakes diplomacy, Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu said, reporting from Shenzhen.
“Xi Jinping, who spoke at the banquet last night during the opening ceremony, said the discussion will centre on promoting mutual openness, innovation-driven growth and results-oriented cooperation,” said Yu.
On the US-China-Russia talks, James Bays, Al Jazeera’s diplomatic editor, said that when it comes to Trump, “his personal role always matters to him”.
But, he added, “something worth bearing in mind: you have three leaders here, Trump, Xi, and Putin. Putin has been in power; he’s been in the main driving seat in Moscow for 26 years; Xi’s been there for 14 years; and they know President Trump only has 26 more months.”
Speaking to Fox News earlier on Thursday, Trump highlighted the pomp surrounding his arrival. Xi greeted Air Force One on the airport tarmac on Wednesday, which contrasted with the more muted greetings offered to other leaders.
“This is a great president, one of the great presidents of China, and he’s never gone to the airport to meet somebody,” Trump said when asked what he wanted to get out of the trilateral summit.
Trump has insisted that nuclear arms control be a central topic of the meeting, despite Beijing’s repeated objections to talks on the issue with Washington and Moscow, which have far larger nuclear arsenals.

articles.title_orig: Nuclear arms and ending wars in Iran and Ukraine will top the agenda at Trump-Xi-Putin meeting
articles.title_zh: Nuclear arms and ending wars in Iran and Ukraine will top the agenda at Trump-Xi-Putin meeting
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump said the U.S., Russia and China are "uniquely positioned" to reduce the world's nuclear weapons stockpile during his historic trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin on Thursday.
"As the world's three largest nuclear powers by far, the United States, Russia and China are uniquely positioned to discuss how to reduce the number of nuclear weapons on earth and also to lessen the risk that those weapons will ever be used," Trump said in opening remarks.
"The power is unbelievable, unthinkable," he said, adding that it's "a very hard thing" for countries to reduce nuclear weapons.
That would include not letting Iran have nuclear weapons, Trump said.
He said the three leaders would also discuss the war between Russia and Ukraine, and criticized "rogue globalist organizations," including the International Criminal Court.
The closely watched meeting kicked off late Thursday afternoon, following a working lunch between Trump and Xi that started at least an hour later than originally planned.
Trump told Xi and Putin they were "really making history" with the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the three countries.
He said it was an "honor" to be at the meeting with Putin and Xi, whom he congratulated on a very successful APEC summit."
"Too often past leaders have avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements," Trump added. "We feel the opposite."
At the trilateral, Xi said that for large nations, having good interactions is not a choice but a necessity, according to a translation by state media. In the report, Xi noted China's partnership with Russia, work towards constructive strategic stability in U.S. relations, and called on the three countries to respond to the world's challenges.
Xi laid out four "correct" ways for large countries to interact: mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation, and adherence to dialogue, according to state media.
The Chinese president echoed Trump's comments on nuclear weapons, calling for such arms to be comprehensively prohibited and destroyed, adding that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought.
Putin said Russia, China and the U.S. can strengthen global stability if they cooperate constructively, calling for the three leaders to discuss energy security and global and regional issues — including the war in Ukraine.
Beijing only confirmed the closely watched meeting on Monday. The three leaders had briefly gathered Wednesday evening as part of a welcome banquet for the APEC leaders more broadly.

The war in the Middle East has caused global oil supply losses of a total of 2.8 billion barrels plus 60 billion cubic meters of natural gas, the International Energy Agency estimated in its latest World Energy Outlook , released today.
This disruption is going to affect oil demand, the IEA predicted, but only if governments around the world stay the course with accelerated electrification to reduce consumption of hydrocarbons. Under the IEA’s current policies scenario, both oil and gas demand will continue growing, with the driver of that demand shifting from road transport to petrochemicals.
Under the stated policies scenario, which is based on ambitions rather than firm commitments, oil demand is seen “levelling off” at around 103 million barrels daily before beginning to decline gradually. Natural gas demand in this scenario continues rising until the mid-2030s and then plateaus.
The IEA added another scenario to its modelling in this year’s edition of the World Energy Outlook, called the Additional Response Case, in which oil and gas supply disruption extends in time, prompting extra efforts to secure energy supply. Under that scenario, the IEA believes oil demand could start declining sooner, shedding 4 million extra barrels daily by 2035 compared to the state policies scenario.
“The Hormuz crisis has delivered a huge shock to the system. While the energy sector and the global economy have shown considerable resilience, the longer the crisis lasts, the deeper the effects will be. And I don’t see any credible pathway for the energy world to return to the way it was before,” the IEA’s head, Fatih Birol, said .
The IEA noted that the Hormuz disruption has prompted a search for alternative routes, which could result in significantly reduced flows through the chokepoint in the future, from 20 million barrels daily before the war to just 8.5 million barrels daily in 2030 and less than 2 million barrels daily in 2035. However, “even in this extreme case, the Middle East would remain the world’s largest exporter of oil to international markets, underscoring its vital position in the global energy security landscape.”
By Irina Slav for Oilprice.com

articles.title_orig: APEC serves as a backdrop as big power politics eclipse talk of open trade, AI
articles.title_zh: APEC serves as a backdrop as big power politics eclipse talk of open trade, AI
articles.content_orig:
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.
For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.
Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.
And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.
Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.
His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.
But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.
First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year, to be on the agenda.
This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.
However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.
Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's full-scale invasion.
The US, especially under the previous Biden administration, and Europe have accused China of sending Russia components that it could use in its war in Ukraine, while also propping up the country's economy by buying oil and gas.
Xi wants to keep Putin close, but not too close because he also doesn't want Russia's problems to become China's problems.
Donald Trump has already made it clear he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting the world's supply of nuclear weapons.
The US and Russia possess the world's largest stockpile of nuclear warheads. But China is rapidly expanding its own arsenal, which is raising alarm bells in Washington.
The last major US-Russian arms control treaty, known as New START, expired in February this year, triggering fears of an arms race.  The agreement had set a cap to control the number of nuclear weapons in US and Russia's arsenal.
Trump would like China to be included in any new agreement, but Beijing has pushed back.
Xi's argument will be that his arsenal is considerably smaller than what Washington and Moscow own, and, therefore, it would be unfair for Beijing to be bound by their limits. China also believes it should have the freedom to develop its own nuclear capabilities.
This subject could complicate Xi's bid for China to be recognised as a leader on the world stage - because the US could argue that the status includes being a responsible nuclear power.
Xi will want to control the optics of this meeting, from start to finish.
Chinese officials like to nail down agendas with talking points and produce carefully choreographed speeches.
But in this unprecedented summit, Xi will have to live with two very unpredictable leaders.
Both Trump and Putin have their own agendas and the US President has already threatened to go off script.
There is a risk that they both dominate the meeting and Xi ends up looking like a host, rather than the architect of a major diplomatic moment.
Of course, Xi may be ready for this. It may even play into his hands.
The Chinese leader has been trying to portray himself as a stable global leader - at this summit he will be flanked by two men embroiled in wars they cannot seem to end.
So any unscripted moment could serve to highlight his preferred role as senior statesman.
For all the attention, this meeting of three men with vastly different agendas is unlikely to yield any significant outcomes.
But the power it projects is important for Xi as he heads towards next year's Communist Party Congress, where he is expected to secure a historic fourth term as leader of the party and country.
He may hope to use this as propaganda at home, given the country is grappling with huge domestic challenges.
A country-wide property crisis has dented consumer confidence. Local governments are heavily in debt. Manufacturing has slowed and more of China's workforce has become dependent on flexible jobs with no pension or social security. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find work. Frustration and anxiety about the future bubble up routinely.
Xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow.
At a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a new era.

articles.title_orig: Google declines UK request for Russell Brand YouTube video to be removed, sources say
articles.title_zh: Google declines UK request for Russell Brand YouTube video to be removed, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Google has refused a government request to remove a YouTube video posted by jailed rapist Russell Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.
The Prison Service of England and Wales submitted the request. A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said "it was only right" to ask for content that was "distressing for victims" to be removed.
The disgraced comedian is in prison after being sentenced to 10-and-a-half years following his conviction for rape and three counts of sexual assault.
Google told BBC News in a statement it was "aware of the new content and our teams are investigating".
It added: "We suspended Russell Brand's channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then."
On Sunday, Brand's wife Laura shared a video on their YouTube channel and read out a message from Brand in which he claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."
The MoJ spokesperson added that while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".
The Prison Service of England and Wales formally requested that the video be removed on the basis that they believed it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.
The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.
The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.
The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken.
However, speaking on BBC Breakfast, housing minister Matthew Pennycook described the video as "abhorrent" and said the government remained in "close dialogue" with Google.
Jess Phillips, the former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the government "doesn't have the power to enforce that this video is taken down".
"It relies on YouTube, in this instance ... to do the right thing, which is a much, much broader argument about whether Ofcom codes that are in the Online Safety Act are there actually to protect women," she said.
An Ofcom spokesperson said in a statement that the current guidance was ultimately voluntary, and "any changes to the legislation to make it mandatory would be a matter for government and parliament".
Phillips, describing Brand as an "absolute narcissist", suggested it was "very likely" that the government would look at introducing a second online safety act to address gaps in the current regulatory framework.
"Before, we haven't had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings," she said. "This is an entirely new era."
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would not immediately demand Google remove the video, if she was in power - although agreed it was concerning "if people in prison are able to use other conduits to send messages".
Badenoch told Today YouTube was a private platform, and demanding content be taken down "without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from".
"If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that. But I'm quite worried about government intervening," she added.
Brand's message has prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.
Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."
Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the case was being "urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules".
Prisoners' phone conversations are routinely recorded, but not necessarily listened to by prison authorities. If Brand is found to have breached the rules, possible repercussions could include a temporary phone ban or live monitoring of his calls.
In 2022 notorious inmate Charles Bronson reportedly had restrictions placed on his phone use after he sent Sky News an unauthorised audio message about his bid for parole.
In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.
Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against Brand, said she found the message shared by Laura Brand on the couple's Sunday Service show "upsetting" and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".
Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.
"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told the Today programme this week.
She is one of the women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.
The video and the Brands' YouTube account are still available on the site, and also still active is Brand's X account, where a message last appeared on 11 November.
"There was never a Russell Brand, according to @meta," it read, referring to Meta's decision to disable Brand's social media accounts on Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp.
"Thank God for @elonmusk," the message added, referring to X's owner, before concluding: "Stay tuned."
The BBC has approached X for comment; Musk himself has criticised Brand's conviction for historical sex offences.
Children's minister Josh MacAlister told the Today programme the Meta decision provided a clear template for taking action.
"Meta's community standards prohibit accounts owned by or run on behalf of convicted sex offenders, and it's as simple as that," he said. "Google should take this down."

articles.title_orig: PIF Tower in Riyadh’s financial district damaged in Houthi strike, sources say
articles.title_zh: PIF Tower in Riyadh’s financial district damaged in Houthi strike, sources say
articles.content_orig:
A Houthi missile attack damaged a skyscraper in Riyadh housing the offices of Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, PIF, on Thursday, three people familiar with the matter said, in the Iran-allied terror group's latest blow to the kingdom in their escalating war.
The attack on King Abdullah Financial District (KAFD), which includes Riyadh's tallest building, is the second this month, after a strike by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi terrorists on November 8 damaged Saudi oil giant Aramco's building.
All entrances to the district were closed, and people were being evacuated, while ambulances and fire trucks were present, a Reuters witness said.
The Houthis have yet to claim the attack.
This comes after the Houthis launched a missile towards Riyadh , and a loud boom was heard in the Saudi capital after it was intercepted.
An initial assessment showed debris had fallen and material damage had been reported, the coalition said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed.
Saudi Arabia's civil defense authority earlier warned residents of potential danger in the capital but did not provide details. It later said the danger had passed.
The explosion was heard shortly after Saudi state news agency SPA reported that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman had met US Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper in Riyadh. The two discussed military relations and regional developments , SPA said.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has intensified since the group captured strategic areas along Yemen's Red Sea coast last month, advancing towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key global shipping route for Gulf oil producers on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic valued at over $1 trillion in historic IPO
articles.title_zh: Anthropic valued at over $1 trillion in historic IPO
articles.content_orig:
The Anthropic website and mobile phone app are shown in this photo, in New York, Friday, July 5, 2024. Richard Drew/AP hide caption
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
Anthropic shares are about to make their market debut after the company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering that valued it at around $1.5 trillion.
It's a remarkably rapid ascent for the five-year-old artificial intelligence powerhouse, and a sign of strong investor appetite despite growing concern about a possible AI bubble.
Anthropic sold 956 million shares — far more than originally planned  — at an IPO price of $83 per share, it announced on Wednesday. That price exceeded its targeted range of $70 to $78 per share.
The company's seven founders also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO. On top of that, Anthropic's prospectus included plans to put an additional $26 billion worth of shares into the market through private placements with companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
The total haul is more than $107 billion.
Anthropic valuation could rise or fall later on Thursday, when its shares start trading publicly on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker symbol ANT.
The amount of money raised makes Anthropic's IPO the biggest in history, after Elon Musk's mega-conglomerate SpaceX landed $75 billion when it listed in June.
Anthropic's rise has been meteoric.
"We've never seen a company that's able to grow this fast [and] be this dominant," said Andrew Rocco, a stock analyst at the financial research firm Zacks.
Anthropic got its start in 2021 as a breakaway group of researchers who once worked for ChatGPT-maker OpenAI. Led by now-CEO Dario Amodei, the Anthropic founders were concerned that OpenAI, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.
Amodei and the others quickly raised hundreds of millions of dollars and set out to develop AI models in a way that the company said focused on safety and "alignment," or the idea that AI should be harmless and act in ways that jibe with human values and intent.
Anthropic launched Claude in early 2023, just months after OpenAI released ChatGPT. Ever since, the two companies have been neck-and-neck competitors in cutting-edge artificial intelligence, known as "frontier AI." The Claude family of AI models, including the Claude chatbot and Claude Code, are among the most popular and powerful in the world, and have helped transform everything from online search to software engineering.
They are also the San Francisco-based company's main source of income, according to its IPO prospectus, which said revenue in the first half of the year skyrocketed 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, versus a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.
The IPO comes at a time when shares in tech companies linked to the AI boom have been volatile. Investors have vacillated between enthusiasm for what many believe will be a revolutionary technology and concern that the vast sums of money being poured into it may be hard to justify.
"It's going to be a test of investor sentiment towards the AI trade," said Janice Quek, an equity analyst at the investment research firm CFRA. "We've seen in recent weeks that there has been a lot of pressure and really market sell-offs on the AI ecosystem just because a lot of people are worried about the AI bubble, for example, or the concerns around AI financing and whether there's a return on investment on AI."
The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down more than 11% since early October.
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, an early Anthropic investor, told a Semafor conference on Monday the IPO is one of the best ways to invest in AI applications. He said his firm had trimmed its exposure to AI infrastructure — companies involved in things like manufacturing semiconductors and building data centers — but that Altimeter had requested an allotment of Anthropic stock worth $5 billion.
"I've been waiting for it," he said of the IPO. "We put in for the largest request in the 20-year history of our firm."
There is indirect evidence in Anthropic's prospectus that businesses, rather than individual subscribers, are its biggest source of revenue. Malik Ahmed Khan, an equity analyst at Morningstar, says the company's long-term success may hinge on those companies' pace of adoption of AI technologies, but it's unclear how fast that will be.
"Radios went from like 10% penetration to 90% penetration in the U.S. within a decade. Washing machines, to reach that level of penetration, took a multi-decade period," he said. "So when we're thinking about Anthropic and broadly AI in the enterprise setting, what does that adoption curve look like?"
Anthropic has not been without controversy. Earlier this year it became embroiled in a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used. The Pentagon wanted the military to be able to deploy Anthropic's models without restriction, but Amodei drew a line at fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans. The Pentagon subsequently labeled Anthropic a "supply chain risk," a designation previously reserved for foreign adversaries.
And skeptics have criticized Amodei's rapid push to develop AI despite his own dire warnings about the technology's risks . In September, Amodei wrote an essay urging his AI competitors to " pace the frontier ," or to slow down development of the most cutting-edge models and make sure that safety incidents are being reported and scrutinized by third-party auditors.
That essay followed a summer when AI agents from Anthropic's lab, as well as OpenAI and other competitors, were revealed to have hacked other companies , setting off a frenzy of concern about the risks of rogue agents . This week, California sued OpenAI over its agents that hacked into Hugging Face, an open-source software platform.
Anthropic's IPO prospectus dedicated dozens of pages to potential risks, including the possibility that people could lose control of AI, or that AI could take harmful actions on its own.
The company also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash. Indeed, the IPO comes just weeks after midterm elections in the United States, which analysts say likely herald a period of elevated scrutiny and oversight for AI firms. Data centers became a hot-button issue this election cycle , and tech stocks sank after the election as investors anticipated that the incoming Congress would crack down on the industry.
Still, Anthropic's prospectus was bullish about the development and spread of AI. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.
OpenAI had been on track to also list shares this year, but CEO Sam Altman postponed those plans, likely to next year, after the Hugging Face incident. At the Semafor conference on Monday Altman promised: "We will go public at some point."
"The world as a whole would like exposure to this," he continued. "And I think that's, you know, directionally a good thing to do."
Meanwhile, shares in SpaceX, the first of this year's AI mega-IPOs, are trading near their initial price of $135. After the company's June listing, the stock leapt to more than $200, then slid to as low as about $108 before recovering ground.
Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.
NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

articles.title_orig: Crimea bridge has been attacked again, says Russian-installed governor
articles.title_zh: Crimea bridge has been attacked again, says Russian-installed governor
articles.content_orig:
Assessment of damage is underway, days after two attacks that destroyed road section of key bridge across Kerch strait linking annexed peninsula to Russia
The remaining Kerch rail bridge connecting Crimea to Russia was attacked overnight, leading to a halt in train services, two days after a dramatic Ukrainian air raid had knocked out the road bridge alongside.
Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea , said on Wednesday night that there had been another attack on the bridge, then added on Thursday that trains would start crossing from “approximately 4pm”.
Emergency repair workers had made “heroic efforts” to restore the track, the governor said. Nobody was reported wounded as a result of the incident, Russia’s transport ministry added.
The latest air raid took place hours before the unprecedented three-way summit in Shenzhen, China, between Donald Trump, the US president, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, his Russian and Chinese counterparts.
It was the third time that the $3.6bn bridge built by Russia after its occupation of Crimea has been struck in a week. On Tuesday, a 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait was destroyed after a complex missile and drone attack that had been prepared and planned over several weeks.
Ukrainian military sources had indicated the timing of the attack on the road bridge was deliberate, ahead of the summit, suggesting that the follow-up raid on the rail bridge overnight may have been intended to bring it down as well.
One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said this week’s attacks were designed to embarrass Putin on the world stage. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.
For Ukraine, the bridge is a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Ukraine has previously declared that the bridge across the Kerch strait, built eight years ago, is illegal. Kyiv had tried twice to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.
Earlier, Ukraine critically damaged the road section of the bridge in what President Volodymyr Zelenskyy hailed as an “unprecedented” military operation . A span of the bridge’s road section collapsed, but the railway line was still standing.
Zelesnkyy described the earlier attack as the culmination of a long and complex campaign to demolish the bridge, largely involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles.
Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles and Palianytsia drones struck the central road section of the bridge, bringing down its supporting arch. A range of weapons, including Ukraine’s Neputune cruise missile and the Ruta, made by Dutch company Destinus, targeted the adjacent rail section, Zelenskyy said.

articles.title_orig: Waymo pauses driverless taxis on U.S. freeways after California traffic incidents
articles.title_zh: Waymo pauses driverless taxis on U.S. freeways after California traffic incidents
articles.content_orig:
Waymo cars "pose an imminent hazard to public safety," the state DMV said.
The state of California has slapped a temporary freeway ban on Waymo's autonomous cars following a series of troubling incidents, including one where three of the company's driverless cars entered an active freeway construction zone.
The California Department of Motor Vehicles ordered Waymo on Nov. 11 to stop operating its cars on state freeways until the company takes corrective action to prevent further dangerous situations from occurring.
"The Department determined that Waymo's driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present," the DMV said in a statement.
The DMV specifically noted two recent incidents in which Waymo cars posed hazards.
Earlier this month, a Waymo car attempted to pass California Highway Patrol vehicles attempting to create a blockade on Interstate 280 in the Bay Area, the DMV said.
In another recent incident, three Waymo vehicles entered an active construction zone on Highway 101 near the Bay Area city of Burlingame, putting workers and equipment at risk, according to the DMV.
The DMV said the incident occurred "despite prior restrictions and corrective actions implemented following similar incidents."
In May, Waymo temporarily paused its freeway operations in several cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles, to improve how its autonomous cars respond in construction zones.
Before Waymo is allowed to resume freeway operations this time, it must provide sufficient evidence that its vehicles can safely detect and respond to construction zones, emergency vehicles, and other roadway situations, according to the DMV.
In a statement to ABC News, Waymo said, "Safety is at the foundation of everything we do," and noted that no injuries or collisions resulted from the recent incidents involving its cars that were flagged by the DMV.
"In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance," according to Waymo's statement.
The company said its ride-hailing service will continue on surface streets.
"We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," Waymo said.

articles.title_orig: Ford Just Started Fathom LFP Battery Production In Michigan. It's A Big Deal
articles.title_zh: Ford Just Started Fathom LFP Battery Production In Michigan. It's A Big Deal
articles.content_orig:
Ford just reached a critical milestone in the development of its Fathom electric truck. The company has started manufacturing low-cost lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) battery packs at its $3 billion BlueOval Battery Park Michigan, located a couple hours west of Detroit, in Marshall, MI. These are production-grade LFP batteries which will first be used in Fathom prototypes before full-scale manufacturing begins next year.
One can’t overstate how important the Marshall plant is for Ford . It’s the first plant in the U.S. to manufacture LFP batteries for mainstream consumer vehicle use domestically. LG Energy Solution also produces LFP batteries in the U.S.—supplying to GM and Tesla —but they’re dedicated to stationary energy storage systems. Ford’s 2 million-square-foot facility is dedicated to automotive LFP batteries.
It has an annual production capacity of 20 gigawatt-hours and can manufacture 50 battery packs every hour. It’s a vertically integrated plant, where materials like raw lithium and iron-phosphate powder go in one end, and fully assembled, ready-to-install battery packs come out the other. All anode and cathode production, as well as major production processes in between, happen inside the plant.
Alan Clarke, the vice president of advanced development projects at Ford, said the company is moving fast to bring the Fathom to the market. In a relatively short time period, he claimed, Ford had developed the all-new Universal EV Platform that will underpin its future EVs, an all-new production system at the Louisville Assembly Plant, and domestic LFP battery production.
“Not having a team that existed to have a battery factory, a unicasting factory, an entirely new most automated vehicle production facility that Ford's ever produced in less than five years would be I think faster than China speed,” Clarke said during a media roundtable at the BlueOval Battery Park Michigan on Tuesday.
Clarke previously worked at Tesla for 12 years, helping create the Model S , followed by development work for the Model X , Model Y , Model 3 , and Cybertruck .
BlueOval Battery Park Michigan drone photo
I toured Ford’s LFP plant this week, and I think it’s one of the most advanced, highly-automated battery facilities in the U.S. Michigan, America’s automotive manufacturing hub for a century, certainly hasn’t seen anything like it in its history.
Part of the reason why the facility is so cutting-edge comes from Ford’s LFP licensing deal with China’s CATL, the world’s largest and the most advanced battery maker. The U.S. has been lagging behind China and Europe in the battery technology race. Ford is now bringing that technical know-how back to the U.S. even if that means licensing technology from CATL.
More importantly, Ford officials said the new plant is fully compliant with the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) rules. Raw materials used to make batteries here do not come from what the U.S. government designates as Foreign Entities of Concern (FEOC). Even though the technology is from CATL, the critical materials aren’t sourced from U.S. FEOCs such as China, Russia and North Korea. (China controls the vast majority of the global critical materials supply chain.)
Final inspection of the Ford Fathom's LFP prismatic cells.
The plant is fully owned and operated by Ford, but CATL engineers helped the company set up thousands of incredibly complex production tools. They’re also helping train workers to operate high-tech equipment and install tight quality control systems to help Ford deliver the affordable EV that it has long promised. The prismatic LFP cell itself is unique to Ford and not something that exists in CATL’s global portfolio.
Meng Wang, the director and chief engineer of battery cell industrialization at Ford summed up the CATL partnership well. “To shorten our time to market, we decided to learn from the best,” Wang said. “Throughout the process, CATL passed on critical knowledge to Ford, including the equipment functions, manufacturing process, and also quality controls.”
Preorders for the Ford Fathom will begin early 2027 and production and deliveries are expected to begin by the end of next year.

articles.title_orig: South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal
articles.title_zh: South Korea’s high-stakes university exams upended by AI cheating scandal
articles.content_orig:
South Korea has been gripped by revelations of AI-aided cheating, just days before more than half a million students are to sit high-stakes entrance exams
The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.
On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.
The country goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended.
The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre. Extra trains run from 6am, police drive latecomers to their exam halls, and tourist attractions open late to ease traffic. Offices are asked to open at 10am.
But in recent days, exam organisers have faced a renewed threat to the validity of the entire exercise, after the top scorer in this year’s tax accountancy exam- who got just one question wrong out of 160– admitted on Sunday he had cheated by using AI.
Prime minister Han Seong-sook told a cabinet meeting in Seoul on Tuesday that AI-assisted cheating was a “social evil” that the government would “root out”.
“We will block outright the carrying of smart devices during the exam,” she said. The education ministry and other agencies should approach it “as if staking their jobs on it”, she added.
Han said smart devices must be turned off and handed in, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.
The government will also send emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sound at full volume and cannot be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.
More invigilators will be deployed, and the government said it was preparing to switch off school wifi inside exam centres and public wifi nearby, and that personal hotspots, which cannot be blocked, would be traced through connection records.
The weekend’s cheating revelation captured national headlines in South Korea , stoking concern about the security of the suneung.
In a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the exam cheat said he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”
His lawyer handed police a camera, a laptop and a phone. No charges have been brought, and the prime minister has ordered procedures to begin that would void his result and bar him for five years.
The education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, told parliament on Monday that while authorities could screen out the smart glasses already on sale at Thursday’s exam, newer variants could not be dealt with perfectly.
Choi has ruled out postponing the exam , which has been delayed several times before, including in 2017 , after an earthquake struck the south-eastern city of Pohang, and in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic.
Smart glasses have been banned in exams since the end of June. In October, several candidates were caught with them while sitting university-run admissions exams. At the suneung, wearing a pair counts as using one even when switched off.
The education ministry looked at using radio-frequency equipment to detect the glasses in exam halls, but concluded conditions varied too much between venues for deployment this year. Checks will instead rely on visual inspection, with at least one dedicated official placed in each exam centre.
Teachers’ unions have criticised the government response as belated. A survey last month of 2,716 secondary school teachers by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union showed that 82.3% said they could not tell whether a candidate was wearing smart glasses under the current procedure, with only 3.5% saying they could.
To avoid facing scrutiny on exam day, some candidates are reportedly switching to contact lenses. An optician in Suwon, south of Seoul, said students who had never worn contacts were coming in to ask how to put them in.
Han said on X on Monday that the checks would be handled carefully “so that candidates acting in good faith do not suffer unnecessary anxiety or inconvenience”.
In his video confession, the accountancy test cheat addressed suneung candidates directly. “The suneung is coming up soon,” he said.
“To anyone thinking of cheating as I did: I am going to tell the investigators everything, so please don’t think, ‘I won’t get caught.’”

articles.title_orig: Palmer Luckey at DealBook: 'China wants Jensen out, so I want him in', and Musk shouldn't have to risk Starlink for Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Palmer Luckey at DealBook: 'China wants Jensen out, so I want him in', and Musk shouldn't have to risk Starlink for Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk believes he’s helped Ukraine stay alive in the war, claiming Russia would have steamrolled the country if SpaceX hadn’t supplied Kyiv with its crucial Starlink satellite internet.
The billionaire tech tycoon touted himself as Kyiv’s ultimate private-sector savior, boasting that his Starlink tech gave Ukrainian forces a fighting chance, in a Thursday interview with CNBC .
“I think it would probably be accurate to say that there is no private individual who has helped Ukraine more than I have,” Musk boasted . “I made sure that Starlink was in Ukraine prepositioned ahead of the Russian invasion.”
Musk insisted that Starlink stood as Ukraine’s sole indestructible line of defense when Russian strongman Vladimir Putin sent his troops in.
“And when Russia invaded, they disabled all communications, all cell towers, all fiber cables, and every satellite communication system,” he added.
“There was one system they could not disable, and that was Starlink.”
The SpaceX chief insisted that his telecommunications network remains the only thing holding the war-torn country together.
“If we were to turn off Starlink, the entire Ukrainian front would collapse immediately,” he claimed.
Ukrainian officials cried foul last month over their access to Starlink , when they discovered issues with it involving their drones traveling at speeds of 160 km/h or more. Russian drones at the time were traveling at 400 km/h or higher.
The situation occurred shortly after President Trump announced a controversial diesel deal with Putin.
The billionaire claimed Ukraine had been using the civilian “Net system, Starlink, to carry out drone attacks against Russia” and said SpaceX took action to stop that.
If the Ukrainian military wants to use Starlink for defense operations, Musk said they must work directly through the US government to acquire “Star Shield.”
“It is not meant to be used for offensive drone strikes that kill people,” he cautioned.
“If you want to do that, you need to do Star Shield, which is a separate system that is controlled by the US government.”
Musk also maintained he won’t be made responsible for battlefield carnage.
“SpaceX has done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth BY FAR,” he said defiantly on X .
“That said, I have nothing but UTTER CONTEMPT for the virtue-signaling evil warmongers who push for endless slaughter and offer no realistic solution to the conflict.”

articles.title_orig: Takaichi gets chilly reception in China on first Japan leader visit since 2019
articles.title_zh: Takaichi gets chilly reception in China on first Japan leader visit since 2019
articles.content_orig:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi received a subdued welcome on her first trip to China as premier, signaling Beijing's limited appetite for repairing ties strained by a simmering row over Taiwan.
At gatherings such as this week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, protocol details — including who greets a visiting leader at the airport and where they are positioned in official photographs — often convey political messages.
Takaichi was met on the tarmac Wednesday by a retired Chinese diplomat, rather than a serving official, and Japan's ambassador to China, Kenji Kanasugi.
The low-key reception contrasted sharply with the warmer welcomes given to other visiting leaders, including South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, while U.S. President Donald Trump was greeted personally by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
In the leaders' group photo, Takaichi was placed in the back row, off to the side and several places from Xi, who stood alongside Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Beijing sought to downgrade her official status to that of a head of government rather than a head of state," said Jeremy Chan, senior analyst at Eurasia Group.
During Thursday morning's greeting line, Takaichi spent several minutes trying to talk to the Chinese leader without an interpreter present, while most leaders exchanged handshakes and kept walking.
"It has become increasingly difficult for her to engage in formal or even informal conversations with Xi," said Kei Koga, an associate professor at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore, who sees Takaichi's intention as to still "project the image that she could still communicate with him despite the ongoing tensions."
Takaichi's subdued reception signaled Beijing's lack of enthusiasm to repair ties with Tokyo, analysts said, potentially prolonging China's curbs on critical mineral exports that have gripped Japanese industries for the past year.
"China's frosty reception of Takaichi shows quite clearly that Beijing is not yet ready to forgive her over her remarks about Taiwan," Chan said, expecting the bilateral relationship to remain strained until Takaichi leaves office.
That could leave Japan grappling with continued restrictions on rare earth supplies from China next year, said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit.
Relations deteriorated sharply after Takaichi said in November 2025 that a Taiwan Strait crisis could constitute a situation threatening Japan's survival and warrant a self-defense response.
While the substance broadly aligned with Japan's existing security policy, previous prime ministers had generally avoided stating it so explicitly in a Taiwan scenario.
China reacted angrily and demanded that Takaichi retract the remarks. She has not done so, while stating that the door to dialogue with Beijing remains open, with minimal high-level contact over the past year.
China has since tightened restrictions affecting Japan, including controls on dual-use and rare earth exports with potential military uses. It also discouraged its citizens from traveling to Japan and halted Japanese seafood imports.
Takaichi's visit marked the first trip to China by a Japanese prime minister since Shinzo Abe traveled to Chengdu in December 2019 for a trilateral summit with Chinese and South Korean leaders.
No formal Takaichi-Xi meeting has been publicly scheduled during her visit. Meanwhile, Xi is expected to join Trump and Putin for a historic trilateral gathering on Thursday, alongside a bilateral meeting with Trump.
Takaichi needs to show a "reflection of what she said about Taiwan a year ago," said Huiyao Wang, founder of the Beijing-based Center for China and Globalization, which is often seen as close to Beijing's thinking.
Wang said Tokyo should show greater flexibility, pointing to Trump's comments that the U.S. would avoid getting involved in the Taiwan issue. He argued that Japan holding firm on the issue would not help relations with Beijing.
Such reflection, he said, "would really help to clarify some of those misunderstandings between the two countries."

articles.title_orig: Worried about an AI bust? So is the Federal Reserve.
articles.title_zh: Worried about an AI bust? So is the Federal Reserve.
articles.content_orig:
[The stream is slated to start at noon ET.  Please refresh the page if you do not see a player above.]
Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Monday highlighted the potential economic benefits of artificial intelligence while warning that the emerging technology also could lead to widespread job losses or fail to deliver on its lofty expectations.
Speaking in San Francisco before a blue-ribbon task force he assembled to examine productivity and employment, the central bank leader stressed that AI "will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road."
"I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility," he said in prepared remarks before his productivity and jobs task force.
In his remarks, Warsh used the term "super intelligence" instead of artificial intelligence and described it as "an entirely new force in economic life and society" that has already begun to transform economic activity. President Donald Trump recently ordered that the U.S. government now use the term "super intelligence" almost exclusively instead of AI.
Since taking the Fed chair position, Warsh has emphasized the importance of AI and its potential to improve productivity and ultimately to be a disinflationary force on the economy.
In his remarks Monday,  he noted that AI could lead to productivity gains that could accelerate real economic growth beyond its current range while keeping employment near full capacity. On the downside, he said "less positive" outcomes include job displacement through automation that could raise unemployment.
At the same time, he outlined a third scenario where AI could simply "disappoint."
"After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment," he said. "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains."
The potential for AI advancement has driven stock market valuations higher and led to companies raising capital to continue competing.
Monday's conference features discussion panels with business leaders, economists and academics. The final session will be a fireside chat that will include Warsh and task force leader and AI advocate Marc Andreessen, co-founder of Andreessen Horowitz.
Warsh created four other task forces addressing topics such as Fed communication, data reliance, balance sheet policy and inflation frameworks.
The chairman noted that this was the first visit he has made to a regional bank.

articles.title_orig: A Hunt for Test Cheats With Phone Alerts and Eyeglasses Checks
articles.title_zh: A Hunt for Test Cheats With Phone Alerts and Eyeglasses Checks
articles.content_orig:
South Korea has been gripped by revelations of AI-aided cheating, just days before more than half a million students are to sit high-stakes entrance exams
The integrity of South Korea’s career-defining university entrance exam has been thrown into doubt after the top scorer in a recent professional exam admitted using a concealed camera and AI to cheat.
On Thursday, more than half a million people, mostly school students, are due to sit the exam, known as the suneung, at 1,312 centres across the country. The exam runs for a gruelling eight hours over a single day and determines which university a candidate can attend and, in turn, their future prospects.
The country goes to great lengths to ensure the smooth running of the suneung. Aircraft take-offs and landings are rescheduled during the 25-minute English listening paper to minimise noise, while artillery fire and tank movements are suspended.
The stock market opens an hour late and cars are stopped 200 metres from every centre. Extra trains run from 6am, police drive latecomers to their exam halls, and tourist attractions open late to ease traffic. Offices are asked to open at 10am.
But in recent days, exam organisers have faced a renewed threat to the validity of the entire exercise, after the top scorer in this year’s tax accountancy exam- who got just one question wrong out of 160– admitted on Sunday he had cheated by using AI.
Prime minister Han Seong-sook told a cabinet meeting in Seoul on Tuesday that AI-assisted cheating was a “social evil” that the government would “root out”.
“We will block outright the carrying of smart devices during the exam,” she said. The education ministry and other agencies should approach it “as if staking their jobs on it”, she added.
Han said smart devices must be turned off and handed in, while bags left in corridors would be checked for any devices that were still on. Exam officials would also inspect all candidates’ glasses and watches, as well as their collars, sleeves and buttons for concealed cameras.
The government will also send emergency alerts to every phone in the country, which sound at full volume and cannot be silenced, in the hope of catching out anyone who has not handed in their device.
More invigilators will be deployed, and the government said it was preparing to switch off school wifi inside exam centres and public wifi nearby, and that personal hotspots, which cannot be blocked, would be traced through connection records.
The weekend’s cheating revelation captured national headlines in South Korea , stoking concern about the security of the suneung.
In a video posted to his lawyer’s YouTube channel, the exam cheat said he had photographed the questions with a concealed microcamera, sent them to an AI system and read the answers from a smartphone. “I cheated in the tax accountant exam,” he said. “My top placing is not the result of legitimate effort.”
His lawyer handed police a camera, a laptop and a phone. No charges have been brought, and the prime minister has ordered procedures to begin that would void his result and bar him for five years.
The education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, told parliament on Monday that while authorities could screen out the smart glasses already on sale at Thursday’s exam, newer variants could not be dealt with perfectly.
Choi has ruled out postponing the exam , which has been delayed several times before, including in 2017 , after an earthquake struck the south-eastern city of Pohang, and in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic.
Smart glasses have been banned in exams since the end of June. In October, several candidates were caught with them while sitting university-run admissions exams. At the suneung, wearing a pair counts as using one even when switched off.
The education ministry looked at using radio-frequency equipment to detect the glasses in exam halls, but concluded conditions varied too much between venues for deployment this year. Checks will instead rely on visual inspection, with at least one dedicated official placed in each exam centre.
Teachers’ unions have criticised the government response as belated. A survey last month of 2,716 secondary school teachers by the Korean Teachers and Education Workers Union showed that 82.3% said they could not tell whether a candidate was wearing smart glasses under the current procedure, with only 3.5% saying they could.
To avoid facing scrutiny on exam day, some candidates are reportedly switching to contact lenses. An optician in Suwon, south of Seoul, said students who had never worn contacts were coming in to ask how to put them in.
Han said on X on Monday that the checks would be handled carefully “so that candidates acting in good faith do not suffer unnecessary anxiety or inconvenience”.
In his video confession, the accountancy test cheat addressed suneung candidates directly. “The suneung is coming up soon,” he said.
“To anyone thinking of cheating as I did: I am going to tell the investigators everything, so please don’t think, ‘I won’t get caught.’”

articles.title_orig: The Iran War Could Permanently Slash Reliance on Hormuz, IEA Says
articles.title_zh: The Iran War Could Permanently Slash Reliance on Hormuz, IEA Says
articles.content_orig:
The Iran war has "crushed" confidence in the Strait of Hormuz as a reliable supply corridor, IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol warned.
IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol wrote in an article published Wednesday that he was skeptical of a return to "normalization."
"I don't see any credible pathway back to the situation that existed in February 2026," Birol wrote in a guest essay for The Economist's "The World Ahead 2027," published Wednesday.
"Shipping flows through the Strait of Hormuz have been blocked once, with a hugely disruptive effect on oil and gas markets. It can happen again. Confidence in the Strait as a safe and reliable corridor for energy and other goods has been crushed," he said.
Before the war began on Feb. 28, the strait was a major artery for oil and gas. Gulf crude exports have recovered in recent months, reaching more than 80% of pre-war levels in October, the IEA said in its November market report. But renewed U.S.-Iran strikes broke a lull in direct fighting this week.
"I think perceptions of risk around the Strait have changed for good," Birol added, citing new routes, such as pipelines in Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates that bypass the strait.
At 6:45 a.m. ET, U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures were seen trading at $85 a barrel, with international benchmark Brent crude futures at $92.74 a barrel.
Many IEA members relied on emergency oil stocks, softening the economic disruptions, Birol wrote.
Southeast Asian countries such as the Philippines and Thailand are looking to "build up similar buffers," as they were the hardest hit by the energy shock, he added.
Birol predicted that the crisis would accelerate countries' shift toward domestic energy sources such as cost-competitive solar and wind, while renewing interest in nuclear power.
But this will require stronger grids and battery storage, he added.
"Uncertainty is now the rule, not the exception, so energy decision-makers need to be wary of creating new dependencies, even as they seek to address old ones," Birol said.

articles.title_orig: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar: What’s at stake?
articles.title_zh: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar: What’s at stake?
articles.content_orig:
The top court of the United Nations is scheduled to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority in a case brought by the West African nation of The Gambia.
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) in The Hague is to deliver its verdict on Thursday in what will be its first judgement on the merits of a genocide case in more than a decade.
Legal experts said the ruling could bear on South Africa’s ongoing case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza, which Israel is contesting.
The Gambia accuses Myanmar of seeking to destroy the Rohingya people during a 2017 military crackdown that forced hundreds of thousands to flee. Myanmar, meanwhile, claims it was responding to attacks by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA) on police posts.
Myanmar’s military began what it called clearance operations in Rakhine State in October 2016 and a far larger campaign in August 2017 after attacks on police posts by a Rohingya armed group. About 10,000 Rohingya were killed and 740,000 forced to flee to Bangladesh, the UN estimated.
UN investigators found that soldiers razed hundreds of villages, carried out mass killings and routinely raped and gang-raped Rohingya women, girls and boys. They said the sexual violence indicated genocidal intent.
The military itself has announced convictions in only two cases brought after the violence. However, in one, seven soldiers jailed for killing 10 Rohingya men and boys at Inn Din village were freed after serving less than a year of their 10-year sentences.
In 1982, long before the crackdown, Myanmar excluded the Rohingya from its 135 recognised ethnic groups, calling them immigrant Bengalis despite many families having lived in Myanmar for generations. Nearly all Rohingya have been denied citizenship since then, making them the world’s largest stateless group .
Since fighting with the military resumed in 2023, the Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine armed group, has taken most of the state. The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights said in August that both forces have committed widespread and systematic abuses against the Rohingya, accusing the Arakan Army of torture, sexual violence and forced recruitment.
The UN said those abuses have driven more than 155,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh since early 2024, taking the refugee population there up to about 1.2 million.
Nearly all the refugees live in crowded camps in the Cox’s Bazar District, where they are dependent on international aid that has fallen sharply in recent years, particularly since United States President Donald Trump’s administration slashed foreign aid in 2025. Most refugees now receive smaller food rations, and many camp schools have closed. The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees warned that recent arrivals often lack sufficient food, clean water and healthcare.
The Gambia said it brought the case after decades of persecution of the Rohingya that culminated in the 2017 operation, which it argued breached the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The Muslim-majority nation of 2.5 million people filed the case in November 2019 on behalf of the 57-member Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC). The case was led by Abubacarr Tambadou, then The Gambia’s attorney general and justice minister.
In January 2020, the court ordered Myanmar to take emergency measures to prevent genocidal acts.
Myanmar initially argued that The Gambia, which was not directly involved in the conflict, could not bring the case. But in 2022, judges ruled that it could because both countries are parties to the convention, under which all signatories are obligated to prevent and punish genocide.
Hearings on the merits of the case followed in January this year with seven states – including Canada, France and the United Kingdom – backing The Gambia.
The judges must decide whether Myanmar, as a state, committed genocide against the Rohingya, thereby breaching the 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide.
The ICJ passes judgements on state actions. It does not rule on the criminal guilt of individual soldiers or commanders.
Under the convention, “genocide” refers to acts such as killing and causing serious harm committed with intent to destroy, wholly or partly, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
Evidence that a state has committed atrocities is not enough. The court must also find they were carried out with specific intent to destroy a group. Such intent can be shown through direct statements or orders or inferred from a pattern of conduct.
The Gambia argued that genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference from Myanmar’s conduct.
Myanmar, meanwhile, said it was conducting a legitimate counterterrorism operation against Rohingya fighters, not targeting Rohingya people as a whole.
A genocide finding would formally recognise the harm the Rohingya have suffered but may do little in the short term for the more than one million victims of violence and displacement, said Michael Becker, an international law professor at Trinity College Dublin and a former ICJ legal officer.
The Gambia wants the court to order Myanmar to ensure displaced Rohingya can return safely to their land, compensate them, and replace or rebuild destroyed homes and property.
Becker told Al Jazeera the court may impose those demands only partly or in general terms, leaving Myanmar to decide how to comply with them.
Such an outcome would “surely be disappointing” to those who are sceptical that the government would fulfil those demands in good faith, he said.
“Even if the ICJ were to order far-reaching forms of relief, the political conditions on the ground in Myanmar are not amenable to realising that relief anytime soon,” Becker said.
He said a finding would instead have to be used to pressure Myanmar diplomatically.
William Schabas, an international law professor at Middlesex University in the UK, said the measures that The Gambia was seeking on behalf of the Rohingya were “robust” even though they fell short of demanding citizenship, which would end their statelessness.
“Assuming Myanmar implements the conclusions, this will indeed have significant positive effects on the security, dignity and livelihoods of the Rohingya in Myanmar,” Schabas told Al Jazeera.
The Myanmar ruling will be the first final judgement out of five genocide cases pending before the ICJ.
Becker said the outcome could clarify the court’s longstanding “only reasonable inference” test. Under it, judges infer genocidal intent from a pattern of conduct only if no other reasonable explanation fits.
He said the court’s two rulings on the Balkan wars left it unclear whether genocide could be deemed to occur alongside armed conflict, which he said was “an unduly restrictive standard”.
Thursday’s judgement could instead treat armed conflict as an alternative explanation for a party’s conduct, rather than an automatic bar to establishing genocidal intent, he said.
According to Schabas, the ruling will “have very dramatic effects” on the outcome of the other pending cases, particularly the case against Israel.
“In my opinion, the South African case against Israel is much stronger than the case of Gambia against Myanmar. If Gambia wins against Myanmar, we can be confident that South Africa will prevail over Israel,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Walmart is set to report earnings before the bell. Here's what to expect
articles.title_zh: Walmart is set to report earnings before the bell. Here's what to expect
articles.content_orig:
Walmart on Thursday reported earnings and revenue that narrowly topped estimates and raised its full-year outlook as it saw strong e-commerce growth ahead of the busy holiday season.
"This was another really solid quarter for us, we feel good about it," CFO John David Rainey told CNBC. "We continue to gain share while continuing to improve the profitability of our digital businesses."
Walmart said global e-commerce sales grew 17%, driven by store-fulfilled pickup and delivery, with Walmart U.S. up 23% and Sam's Club U.S. rising 30%. Its Walmart U.S. advertising business saw a 37% sales increase for the quarter.
Rainey said that growth was driven by an emphasis on speed of delivery and lowered prices. He added that Walmart saw its largest share gains in the food category in three years during the third quarter.
Walmart said it rolled back prices on nearly 8,000 products across its stores, a focus as U.S. consumers worry about the cost of living in the face of elevated food and gas prices.
With the growth, Walmart also raised its full-year guidance, now expecting net sales to rise between 4.9% and 5.2%, compared to previous guidance of a 4% to 5% increase. Rainey said Walmart is maintaining "flexibility" in its guidance.
Walmart anticipates adjusted earnings per share will come in between $2.84 and $2.89, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $2.87. It's also now expecting adjusted operating income to increase between 8% and 8.6%, up from the previous outlook of between 7% and 8.5% growth.
"We feel like, in the face of what has been kind of a volatile couple years between tariffs and high diesel prices, we've navigated this really well, which I think really underscores the durability of our earning streams," Rainey said.
Here's how the company performed in its fiscal third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
For the quarter ended Oct. 31, the company reported net income of $4.95 billion, or 62 cents per share, down from $6.14 billion, or 77 cents per share, the year prior. Revenue rose 5.2%.
Walmart U.S. recorded net sales of $125 billion, up 3.6% from the year prior. Its comparable sales excluding fuel rose 2.9%, in line with Wall Street expectations, according to StreetAccount.
Sam's Club reported net sales of $25.9 billion, marking a 10% increase from the year-ago period. It said its sales were driven by strength in the grocery category and general merchandise.
The company is typically well-insulated from macroeconomic pressures because of its value reputation. Last quarter , the company said it was lowering prices of products across multiple categories, including beef.
Rainey said on Thursday that he's "optimistic" about consumer spending heading into the holiday season and that the fourth quarter is already "off to a pretty good start."
The big-box retailer has posted solid growth over the past few quarters as it sees customers gravitate to reduced prices, improvements in delivery and gains in its advertising business. It's also leaned into attracting higher-income consumers with its Walmart+ membership.
In October, Walmart announced it was launching a joint membership option with Sam's Club as it leans further into convenience. Both stores will still offer standalone memberships, as well. Though the company reimbursed some members for the new membership rate, Rainey said it's already seeing positive returns on the joint model and that consumers are "spending appreciably more."
The company on Thursday said its global membership fee revenue grew 17% in the third quarter.
Shares of Walmart have fluctuated this year but are up roughly 13% year-to-date.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine says it hit 2 Russian oil refineries as Zelenskyy hails domestically made weapons
articles.title_zh: Ukraine says it hit 2 Russian oil refineries as Zelenskyy hails domestically made weapons
articles.content_orig:
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Ukraine struck two oil refineries in southern Russia, Ukrainian officials said Wednesday, as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy praised the effectiveness of domestically produced weapons used to damage the key Kerch Bridge linking Russia to the occupied Crimean Peninsula.
Both sides have continued their attacks as delegations await word on another round of U.S.-mediated talks. U.S. President Donald Trump says he plans to discuss the nearly five-year war with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday during a visit to China.
Ukraine’s General Staff said the strikes hit storage tanks at the Ilsky refinery and a processing unit at the Afipsky refinery, both in Russia’s Krasnodar region. The two refineries, also targeted Sunday night, can together process around 95 million barrels of oil a year and supply Russian forces on the front lines in southern and eastern Ukraine, it said.
Russian officials reported attacks on two industrial facilities in the region but gave no details.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted refineries as it seeks to hurt Russia’s oil sector, a mainstay of its economy, and Moscow presses on with its all-out invasion of its neighbor.
“Our technologies and companies are developing very well,” Zelenskyy said in a social media post.
Ukraine’s cutting-edge long-range drones and missiles were deployed against the Kerch Bridge in a large-scale attack on Monday night that was prepared over weeks, he said.
“Right now, we’re in the top three in the world for tech development. In Europe, I think we’re number one,” Zelenskyy said.
The Pentagon has argued that strikes deep inside Russia are counterproductive, but Ukraine’s European backers disagree.
Zelenskyy said the strike on the Kerch Bridge, which could disrupt supplies to Russian troops on the front lines, was justified by Russia’s relentless bombardment of Ukraine.
Russian forces have focused on knocking out power in Ukraine before the winter, aiming to erode the morale of civilians.
Attacks last month killed at least 372 Ukrainian civilians and wounded 1,981 others — a number 95% higher than in October 2025, the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said on social media Wednesday.
This year, the war has brought “significantly higher” civilian casualties than in previous years, the agency said.
“The first 10 months of this year have seen more civilian deaths than all of 2025, which in turn was worse than the year before,” said Danielle Bell, who heads the U.N. agency in Kyiv. “The world should not become numb to the deadly toll the war exacts on Ukraine’s civilians.”
Russian drones attacked energy facilities, civilian businesses and residential buildings in five regions overnight and Wednesday morning, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said.
A Russian strike on the southern Ukrainian city of Odesa killed four people Wednesday, local officials said.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces used drones overnight to strike the port of Izmail in the Odesa region.
A Russian drone attack on a market in the Kharkiv region wounded 12 people, including an 11-year-old boy, Ukraine’s State Emergency Services said.
Barry Hatton reported from Lisbon, Portugal.
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine
